title: B.D.O.C.

jokes.text: The family's farewell gift is revealed to be beer and a fake ID
jokes.setup: The family says they shopped for hours to get Tommy the right thing for college, building expectation of a heartfelt or practical gift
jokes.punchline: It's beer and a fake ID — the alien family's warped but earnest understanding of human college culture
jokes.explanation: Works because it's character-specific — aliens who studied humans would absolutely conclude beer and a fake ID are college essentials. The 'shopped for hours' setup earns the punchline. Solid opening joke.

jokes.text: Yeah. Plus I don't have to live with you freaks anymore, you know?
jokes.setup: The family delivers a heartfelt send-off about exploring new horizons and understanding humanity
jokes.punchline: Tommy deflates the moment by noting the practical bonus of escaping his weird alien family
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom deflation of a sentimental moment. Economy is excellent — 'you freaks' does a lot of work. Not highly original but well-executed for the show's rhythm.

jokes.text: "and help us to further understand that curious race we call human"
jokes.setup: Dick is giving a warm, fatherly send-off speech about college
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals the alien surveillance mission as a parenthetical college benefit
jokes.explanation: Classic 3rd Rock joke structure — the aliens slip their true mission language into mundane moments. The phrase 'that curious race we call human' is perfectly delivered as an afterthought, which is the show's signature comedic register. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hey. Ah-choo! No, not cry. Sneeze.
jokes.setup: Dick says 'I feel like I'm gonna cry' in a touching farewell moment
jokes.punchline: He immediately sneezes and corrects himself — 'No, not cry. Sneeze.' — refusing to show emotion under the guise of physical correction
jokes.explanation: Dick's emotional repression is classic character comedy. The physical interruption of a tender moment with a sneeze, followed by the deadpan correction, is tightly constructed. Character-specific — Dick would absolutely deny vulnerability.

jokes.text: Replacement interviewees are already waiting as Tommy tries to say goodbye
jokes.setup: Tommy asks how they'll ever replace him in an emotional farewell
jokes.punchline: Before he can finish answering, Dick reveals they're already interviewing replacements — candidates are literally walking in the door
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the question 'how will we ever replace you?' is immediately answered visually before the sentence finishes. The cut to interviewees walking in is perfectly timed and brutally funny in how it undercuts Tommy's importance. Rewatch bonus because you appreciate the timing more when you know the reveal is coming.

jokes.text: You hear that? She's gonna somethin' the mission's whatever.
jokes.setup: Christie impresses with corporate buzzword speak: 'leverage my skill set to maximize the mission's effectiveness'
jokes.punchline: Dick summarizes it as 'she's gonna somethin' the mission's whatever' — perfectly capturing that corporate speak is meaningless
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally economical. Dick's alien literalism strips corporate jargon to its essential meaninglessness in six words. Highly quotable, character-specific (only an alien outsider would cut through the BS this precisely), and the joke rewards the audience for recognizing the truth in it. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: So, uh, can we reach you at the transmitter in your head?
jokes.setup: Dick wraps up the professional interview with Christie by saying they'll be in touch
jokes.punchline: He asks if they can reach her at the transmitter in her head — normalizing alien communication technology in a mundane HR context
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist joke — the juxtaposition of formal interview procedure with alien telepathy. Works because it's delivered with complete sincerity, as if this is a perfectly normal HR question.

jokes.text: So, uh, Christie, how you gettin' along with your body? You like the boobs? / No. No, I really don't. / Mmm. Yeah. The smaller ones aren't as much fun.
jokes.setup: Dick asks Christie a personal question about her physical form — framed as a professional concern about adjusting to a human body
jokes.punchline: She doesn't like her boobs; Dick empathizes with 'the smaller ones aren't as much fun' — delivered as alien wisdom, not harassment
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Dick's complete innocence about the inappropriateness of the question, and his comparative expertise on human anatomy as an alien researcher. 'The smaller ones aren't as much fun' is delivered as pure scientific observation, which is what makes it funny rather than offensive. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: "You're hired." — Dick hires Bryce before asking a single question, solely on appearance
jokes.setup: They've just agreed to crank through the remaining candidates since Christie is their pick
jokes.punchline: Bryce walks in and Dick immediately hires him without a word of interview
jokes.explanation: The speed of the hire — instantly, on looks — is the joke. Works as a quick beat. Sally's accusation of 'pretty boy' favoritism and the subsequent 'one question' deflection add good layers.

jokes.text: Bryce, when can you start? / Now. / That is the greatest answer to any question I have ever...
jokes.setup: Dick defends hiring Bryce on looks by offering one token question — 'when can you start?'
jokes.punchline: Bryce says 'Now.' Dick's hyperbolic reaction ('greatest answer to any question I have ever...') is cut off, suggesting he's so overwhelmed he can't finish
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of Dick's reaction is the joke. 'Greatest answer to any question I have ever' being cut off works because the audience imagines the grandiosity of what he was about to say. Economy is excellent — less is more here.

jokes.text: These walls are real cinder block. / Oh, I don't think so. / Dear god, they are!
jokes.setup: Tommy and Dick arrive at his dorm room and Tommy notices the cinder block walls
jokes.punchline: Dick's initial skepticism ('Oh, I don't think so') followed by his shock ('Dear god, they are!') — treating dorm architecture as an alarming discovery
jokes.explanation: Dick's alien outsider perspective transforms mundane dorm observations into genuine discovery. 'Dear god, they are!' treats cinder blocks as an existential revelation. Good character integration — Dick's alien literalism is the engine of the joke.

jokes.text: I know he's unconscious, but I really get that kinda buddies-for-life vibe, you know?
jokes.setup: Tommy's roommate Joel is passed out drunk with Kahlua and Crème; Tommy should be concerned
jokes.punchline: Tommy chooses to read the unconscious stranger's energy positively — 'buddies-for-life vibe' — as if this is a normal way to make friends
jokes.explanation: Tommy's earnest optimism about his passed-out roommate is a nice character beat. The specificity of 'buddies-for-life vibe' from an unconscious person is absurd and efficient. Good economy.

jokes.text: 5, if you're doin' it right.
jokes.setup: Dick tearfully says 'I'll see you in 4 years'
jokes.punchline: Tommy corrects it to 5, implying college should take 5 years if done properly — a classic college joke delivered with alien precision
jokes.explanation: Economical college joke — perfectly placed and efficient. Not highly original (it's a familiar trope) but the timing is good and Tommy's deadpan delivery suits him. 'if you're doin' it right' does all the heavy lifting.

jokes.text: Dick's farewell speech trails off awkwardly when Tommy hints Dick should reciprocate the sentiment of learning from him
jokes.setup: Dick delivers a heartfelt speech about everything he learned from Tommy; Tommy says if Dick wanted to say he learned from Tommy too, that would be fine
jokes.punchline: Long pause. Dick reluctantly says 'Uh... I mean, I must've learned something.' — a non-compliment that barely clears the floor
jokes.explanation: Classic Dick character comedy — his ego prevents him from giving a genuine compliment even in an emotional farewell. The pause and the weak hedge ('I must've learned something') are perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: get around in cars, which have 4 wheels. Humans... have no wheels.
jokes.setup: Bryce is supposed to deliver insightful information about humans to the alien team
jokes.punchline: His 'research' is breathtakingly basic: cars have wheels, humans don't. Delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The pause between 'Humans...' and 'have no wheels' is where the joke lives — Bryce building to a revelation that is absolutely not a revelation. The dramatic structure of a nothing discovery is well-executed. 'Humans have no wheels' has genuine quotability.

jokes.text: Yeah! We've known that for weeks, Bryce.
jokes.setup: Bryce delivers the earth-shattering revelation that humans have no wheels
jokes.punchline: Harry shoots it down immediately: 'We've known that for WEEKS, Bryce' — the 'weeks' implying this was once a breakthrough but has since been surpassed
jokes.explanation: The callback to Bryce's bad intel is enhanced by 'weeks' — implying that 'humans have no wheels' WAS cutting-edge information weeks ago, which makes the alien researchers seem even more ridiculous. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: New guy, new guy, New guy! You've gotta be more specific! / What side of the Road? / Well, the factory's on the left side of the road and... / No! It's too late now!
jokes.setup: Bryce is giving the address of the bagpipe factory
jokes.punchline: Harry demands more specificity about which side of the road, then immediately declares 'It's too late now!' when Bryce tries to answer — absurd urgency about completely useless information
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The absurd escalation of urgency around bagpipe factory geography, culminating in 'It's too late now!' — as if a window of opportunity has closed — is perfectly constructed. The joke escalates in two beats: first the desperate demand for specificity, then the immediate dismissal. 'It's too late now!' is highly quotable out of context and lands as a genuine surprise.

jokes.text: Oops. I dropped my pencil. / Oops. / Oop... hey!
jokes.setup: Sally has been ogling Bryce throughout the scene; now she 'accidentally' drops her pencil to get him to bend over
jokes.punchline: She drops it again ('Oops'), and then appears to be caught in the act on the third attempt ('Oop... hey!')
jokes.explanation: Classic running gag structure — the triple repetition with escalating blatancy. The joke is in Sally's complete lack of subtlety. Not highly original (gender-flipped version of a stock gag) but character-appropriate and the third beat landing on 'hey!' suggests she's been caught, which adds a nice capper.

jokes.text: Dick greets Tommy warmly, then immediately calls him Bryce — forgets his own son
jokes.setup: Dick greets 'Tommy' warmly, then introduces Bryce canyon as the new information officer
jokes.punchline: He calls Tommy 'Bryce' — instantly mixing up his son with his replacement — and doesn't notice
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Dick's self-absorption means he's already mentally replaced Tommy. The obliviousness is the joke.

jokes.text: Say, have you met Bryce canyon, our new information officer? / Oh, hello, Tommy. / Bryce.
jokes.setup: Dick introduces Bryce to a colleague
jokes.punchline: Mary/colleague responds 'Oh, hello, Tommy' — calling Bryce by Tommy's name, showing how replaceable/interchangeable the position is
jokes.explanation: Nice structural joke — Tommy was just being replaced and now someone already confuses the new guy for Tommy. Reinforces the theme of replacability. Simple but effective.

jokes.text: Say, Bryce, we need some sunbathing information. What do you say you grease up, hit the rooftop, and I'll check on your progress later, huh?
jokes.setup: Dick frames ogling Bryce as official information-gathering
jokes.punchline: 'Grease up, hit the rooftop, and I'll check on your progress' is presented as a legitimate work assignment but is transparently an excuse to watch Bryce sunbathe
jokes.explanation: Dick's ability to cloak personal interest in professional language mirrors the later Sally harassment subplot. The 'check on your progress' is the punchline — framing sunbathing as a monitored work activity. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Don't you dare say that. That's Tommy's chair. That'll always be Tommy's chair. He's not dead. He's just in a different location! That's all!
jokes.setup: Dick corrects a colleague who has noted someone is sitting in what used to be Tommy's chair, saying it's 'Bryce's chair now'
jokes.punchline: Dick's emotional escalation — 'That's Tommy's chair. That'll always be Tommy's chair. He's not dead. He's just in a different location!' — reveals his grief about Tommy leaving
jokes.explanation: 'He's not dead. He's just in a different location!' is the standout line — Dick's alien framing of human distance as analogous to death (or the opposite) is character-specific and genuinely funny. The escalation from 'it's Tommy's chair' to 'HE'S NOT DEAD' is well-paced and quotable.

jokes.text: Bryce sunbathing under a desk lamp in the office instead of going to the roof
jokes.setup: Dick has sent Bryce to the roof to sunbathe for 'research'; Harry notices a light in the office
jokes.punchline: Bryce is lying under a small desk lamp inside, apparently substituting it for the roof — Harry's observation 'see, this is the kind of information we need' suggests he accepts this completely
jokes.explanation: This is primarily a visual gag — Bryce lying under a desk lamp is inherently absurd. Harry's acceptance of this as useful research adds a second layer. Works better on screen than on the page.

jokes.text: See, Harry, this is the kind of information we need. [Harry watching Bryce lie in a sunbeam]
jokes.setup: Harry claims they need information from Bryce
jokes.punchline: The 'information' is just watching Bryce sunbathe — Harry frames voyeurism as field research
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the 'information officer' conceit — the show keeps mining the gap between the title and what they actually do. The visual of Harry watching Bryce bathe in a sunbeam while calling it research is the joke.

jokes.text: Dick showing up in Tommy's dorm room uninvited — Tommy's girlfriend dismisses Dick as 'cute' and leaves
jokes.setup: Tommy introduces Dick as his dad to Cindy
jokes.punchline: Cindy says 'that's cute' with thinly veiled dismissal and immediately exits, clearly marking Tommy as a dork
jokes.explanation: The social humiliation is clear and earned — Dick appearing at college immediately tanks Tommy's cool. 'That's cute' as a dismissal is well observed. The joke is more situational than line-driven.

jokes.text: Your dad? That's cute. See ya.
jokes.setup: Tommy introduces Dick as his dad to Cindy, a girl he clearly likes
jokes.punchline: Cindy dismisses Dick with 'that's cute' and immediately leaves — Dick being there has killed Tommy's game
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient joke about a father embarrassing his college-age kid. Nothing groundbreaking but economically executed. 'That's cute' as a total brush-off lands cleanly.

jokes.text: See ya later, cind. / See ya later, cind.
jokes.setup: After Cindy brushes them off, Dick says 'See ya later, Cind' in a casual attempt to seem cool
jokes.punchline: Tommy repeats the exact same line — both of them mimicking each other's cringe attempt to be cool with Cindy
jokes.explanation: The repeated line shows Dick and Tommy are more similar than Tommy wants to admit — both equally awkward. Works as a quick character beat. The repetition itself is the joke.

jokes.text: I think she thinks you're a dork.
jokes.setup: Dick just tried to be cool in front of Cindy
jokes.punchline: Tommy's flat observation — delivered as news, not accusation — is funnier than any elaborate insult would be
jokes.explanation: Economy carries this one — 'I think she thinks you're a dork' is precisely calibrated. The use of 'dork' rather than something harsher is perfectly Tommy. Not a high-craft joke but functionally effective.

jokes.text: Oh, no, but it's gotten much better. We just painted.
jokes.setup: Dick is trying to convince Tommy to come home and attend Pendleton community college, which Tommy has criticized for years
jokes.punchline: 'We just painted' as the primary evidence that Pendleton has 'gotten much better' — a completely inadequate improvement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The specificity of 'we just painted' as the grand improvement to a college Tommy has hated for six years is perfectly absurd and pathetic. Dick's earnestness makes it land. The economy is exceptional — four words do enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: Dick's argument for Tommy not going to Pendleton: 'We just painted.'
jokes.setup: Dick is trying to convince Tommy to come back home and go to local Pendleton college, which Tommy has called terrible for years
jokes.punchline: Dick's improvement to justify Pendleton: 'Oh, no, but it's gotten much better. We just painted.' — an absurdly inadequate upgrade
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'We just painted' as the lone justification for a college's improvement is perfectly absurd. The understatement is weaponized — the more banal the improvement, the funnier. Pure economy: three words, big laugh. Very quotable, very Dick.

jokes.text: that wreaks havoc, but makes you the most popular man on campus.
jokes.setup: Dick mentions the 'freshman prank' as something Tommy should do
jokes.punchline: Dick defines it as something that 'wreaks havoc but makes you the most popular man on campus' — an alien's confident but slightly off understanding of college social dynamics
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — Dick's alien confidence about human social rituals he doesn't fully understand. Sets up the prank subplot more than it lands as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Look at your friend Cindy, talking to that young rascal over there. I wonder what sort of Freshman prank he's cooking up.
jokes.setup: Dick is trying to manipulate Tommy into doing the prank by making him jealous of Cindy's attention toward another guy
jokes.punchline: Dick frames the rival's appeal as purely prank-related — 'what sort of freshman prank he's cooking up' — either missing or deliberately weaponizing Tommy's jealousy
jokes.explanation: Dick's manipulation of Tommy via Cindy jealousy while staying in the 'freshman prank' framing is nicely character-specific. The ambiguity of whether Dick understands what he's doing (or is being calculating) is the comedy engine.

jokes.text: Harry waiting over an hour for a mustard report while his pastrami goes uneaten — treating mustard selection as a military information crisis
jokes.setup: Harry confronts Bryce about the delayed mustard report
jokes.punchline: Harry frames the unsanctioned pastrami as a national security situation requiring immediate intelligence on mustard
jokes.explanation: Harry treating mustard selection with the same gravity as a military intelligence operation is absurdist comedy that fits his character perfectly. The specificity of 'pastrami and cheese' that's 'not getting eaten' adds texture.

jokes.text: Harry's mentorship advice: "Get comfortable in your own skin." / Bryce: "About that... it feels so tight, especially under the arms."
jokes.setup: Harry gives standard mentorship advice to 'get comfortable in your own skin'
jokes.punchline: Bryce takes it literally — his human skin physically fits poorly, especially under the arms
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The idiom 'get comfortable in your own skin' lands perfectly when taken literally by a new alien inhabiting a human body for the first time. 'Especially under the arms' is the specific detail that elevates it from a simple literalism joke to genuine wit — it sounds exactly like a complaint about an ill-fitting garment. Structure is impeccable: setup the idiom, pause, literal interpretation, precise physical detail.

jokes.text: Gum can double as adhesive, but most adhesives do not necessarily double as gum.
jokes.setup: Dick is mentoring Bryce, dispensing wisdom
jokes.punchline: His advice veers into absurd specificity: gum as adhesive vs. adhesive as gum — delivered as a profound life lesson
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and among the show's finest absurdist one-liners. It works on multiple levels: (1) It's structurally valid — gum IS adhesive but not vice versa — so it has the form of wisdom. (2) It's delivered as profound mentoring advice. (3) It's completely useless as life advice while somehow feeling meaningful. (4) The economy is perfect — not a single wasted word. (5) It's extraordinarily quotable and sounds profound out of context. Easily the most quotable line in the episode and comparable to the '8.0 anchor' examples given for calibration — genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: Harry's Vaseline advice for tight alien skin
jokes.setup: Bryce complains his skin is tight under the arms
jokes.punchline: Harry recommends Vaseline as the solution — 'just lube them bad boys up, they work all day' — treating human skin maintenance like machinery
jokes.explanation: The mechanical framing of human joints ('lube them bad boys up') is funny and character-appropriate. Works as a callback payoff to the skin joke above, though stands slightly lower because the setup joke is stronger.

jokes.text: No. No. You don't have to call me 'Sir.' Call me 'Your honor.' / Your honor. / Yeah. Little bit louder. / Your honor. / That's it.
jokes.setup: Dick tells Bryce not to call him 'Sir' in a seemingly humble gesture
jokes.punchline: He insists on 'Your Honor' instead — a title that is MORE formal and pompous than 'Sir' — and then coaches Bryce to say it louder
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally character-specific joke — Dick's grandiosity disguised as false modesty. The escalation from 'you don't have to call me Sir' (implying humility) to 'call me Your Honor' (implying the opposite) is a perfect misdirection. The coaching — 'little bit louder' — turns it into a self-aggrandizing performance ritual. This is Dick Solomon at his most Dick. Strong craft across the board.

jokes.text: Dick, open the door. / You have the... You have the doorknob. / I know. / Oh, my god! You planned this. You're trying to get me expelled! / Bingo!
jokes.setup: Dick convinced Tommy to remove the doorknob as part of a prank, then they are trapped inside
jokes.punchline: 'Bingo!' — Dick reveals the entire prank was a setup to get Tommy expelled so he'd have to come home. The whole sequence was a long con
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's structural comedy highlight. 'Bingo!' is the perfect single-word punchline to a long con that retroactively reframes the entire prank sequence as Dick's elaborate manipulation. The structure is excellent: Dick plants the idea, engineers the prank, suggests removing the doorknob, and the trap springs. 'Bingo!' does enormous work in one word — it's proud, cheerful, and completely unrepentant. The rewatch value is high because every step of the prank sequence now reads as intentional. Among the episode's top two or three moments.

jokes.text: And that's why old men wear their pants higher than young men. That is fantastically useful.
jokes.setup: Bryce has apparently been presenting research findings to Sally late at night
jokes.punchline: The research he's been sharing is 'why old men wear their pants higher than young men' — Sally calls it 'fantastically useful' with no apparent sarcasm, which is its own joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the scale mismatch — Sally has kept Bryce up all night for 'research' that turns out to be trouser height patterns. 'Fantastically useful' is either Sally not caring about the information at all (just wanting Bryce there) or genuinely alien enthusiasm for trivial human data. Either reading is funny.

jokes.text: 'Sally's boy wonder,' that's what they're calling you. / Who's calling me that? / Sally.
jokes.setup: Sally tells Bryce he's making a name for himself — 'Sally's boy wonder' — implying broad recognition
jokes.punchline: Bryce asks who's saying this; the answer is only Sally herself — she invented her own flattering nickname for Bryce
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy joke. Three lines, two beats, reveals Sally's self-serving harassment through comic misdirection. The structure is textbook: setup implies social validation ('they're calling you'), question creates expectation of outside confirmation, punchline deflates entirely — 'Sally.' alone is the punchline word. Highly quotable, completely character-specific. One of the episode's sharpest constructed jokes.

jokes.text: Sally describes Bryce as 'Sally's boy wonder' — and when Bryce asks who calls him that, Sally says 'Sally'
jokes.setup: Sally tells Bryce he's making a name for himself — 'Sally's boy wonder, that's what they're calling you'
jokes.punchline: Bryce asks 'Who's calling me that?' and Sally replies simply 'Sally.' — revealing she invented and is the sole user of her own nickname for him
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The setup implies broad organizational praise, making the collapse to 'Sally' (referring to herself in third person as the sole source) perfectly timed. Maximum economy — two words detonate the joke. Strong character integration: Sally's self-aggrandizing obliviousness is a perfect character beat.

jokes.text: "My research tells me that alcohol dulls your senses and impairs your judgment." / "I had not heard that."
jokes.setup: Sally pours Bryce a glass of wine as a prelude to seduction
jokes.punchline: Bryce cites research on alcohol's effects; Sally's 'I had not heard that' is a perfect deadpan lie
jokes.explanation: Sally's 'I had not heard that' is a gloriously straight-faced lie — everyone knows alcohol impairs judgment, especially someone trying to use it for seduction. The formal phrasing 'I had not heard that' rather than 'really?' or 'huh' elevates it.

jokes.text: How far? All the way... but that's just the beginning. / How can 'All the way' be just the beginning?
jokes.setup: Sally tells Bryce he has a chance to 'go far' in the organization
jokes.punchline: She says 'all the way... but that's just the beginning' — clearly using professional language as a sexual double entendre. Bryce's literal/innocent response ('How can all the way be just the beginning?') is its own comedic beat
jokes.explanation: The double entendre is reasonably clever, but what elevates it is Bryce's literal response. He genuinely can't parse the innuendo and responds logically to the semantic impossibility. This mirrors the alien-outsider comedy throughout the episode.

jokes.text: I like the way you think, Bryce... but you can stop now.
jokes.setup: Bryce has been pushing back logically on Sally's innuendos
jokes.punchline: Sally gives a backhanded compliment ('I like the way you think') then immediately shuts down actual thinking in favor of her agenda
jokes.explanation: Efficient character joke — Sally's interest in Bryce has nothing to do with his analytical abilities. 'But you can stop now' is the perfectly calibrated punchline. Good economy.

jokes.text: This chair isn't very comfortable. I want to sit where you're sitting. / No. No. No. Don't get up.
jokes.setup: Sally has been making increasingly transparent moves on Bryce
jokes.punchline: She uses the pretense of chair comfort to try to get Bryce to move — presumably so she can sit on his lap or engineer physical contact. 'No. No. No. Don't get up.' makes her intentions obvious
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy beat in the Sally/Bryce harassment subplot. The transparent pretext (chair comfort) and her immediate reversal when Bryce moves to get up reveals the actual goal. Competent but not the subtlest version of this joke type.

jokes.text: Well, Uh, uh, traffic lights. Green means 'Go.' / Aah! / You cracked the code. Let's celebrate.
jokes.setup: Sally enthusiastically asks for Bryce's research, implying she wants important information
jokes.punchline: Bryce reveals traffic light data — 'green means go' — as if it's a discovery. Sally's 'You cracked the code!' and 'Let's celebrate' is sarcastic but also transparently an excuse to drink with Bryce
jokes.explanation: 'You cracked the code' for figuring out traffic light colors is a nice callback to the show's ongoing joke about trivial discoveries. 'Let's celebrate' immediately pivoting to drinking shows Sally doesn't care about the research at all. Good rhythm in this exchange.

jokes.text: I'm beginning to wonder if you care about traffic lights at all!
jokes.setup: Sally has been trying to get Bryce to drink wine and stay late; Bryce has been obliviously giving traffic light research
jokes.punchline: Bryce accuses Sally of not caring about traffic lights — his innocent framing makes him sound like a jilted researcher, completely missing the actual dynamic
jokes.explanation: Excellent line — Bryce's alien literalism cuts through the entire harassment subplot in one sentence. He's completely right but spectacularly wrong about what's happening. 'I'm beginning to wonder if you care about traffic lights at all!' is highly quotable and absurd enough to work out of context. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Sure. Blame dad.
jokes.setup: Tommy has been yelling 'You set me up, you bastard!' at Dick in front of the college chancellor
jokes.punchline: Dick's casual 'Sure. Blame dad.' — entirely unbothered and slightly martyred, as if Tommy's accusation of getting him deliberately trapped is an unfair characterization
jokes.explanation: After 'Bingo!' confirmed Dick's guilt, 'Sure. Blame dad.' is the perfect follow-up — Dick playing the wounded parent despite having literally admitted to the scheme moments earlier. The irony is thick and delivered with perfect deadpan. Economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Well, it is a serious offense. Where are the expulsion forms, in your desk? I could give you a leg up.
jokes.setup: The chancellor has just issued Tommy only a warning; Dick expected and hoped for expulsion
jokes.punchline: Dick actively offers to help the chancellor find the expulsion forms — working against his own son's interests in order to bring him home
jokes.explanation: 'I could give you a leg up' is the killer phrase — Dick cheerfully offering assistance to expel his own son. The character logic is perfect: Dick's love for Tommy manifests as trying to get him thrown out of college. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: But a warning? Why don't you just give him a big wet kiss?
jokes.setup: The chancellor defends his lenient response as supporting 'youthful exuberance'
jokes.punchline: Dick's sarcastic escalation — 'why don't you just give him a big wet kiss?' — framing mercy toward Tommy as embarrassing coddling
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Dick's indignation at Tommy's lenient punishment is funny because it's the opposite of a parent's normal reaction. The phrase itself ('big wet kiss') is reasonably funny. Not the sharpest joke in the sequence.

jokes.text: Dean bonds with Dick over his own freshman prank: making a marching band spell out a dirty word — but the Dean thinks Dick's prank was MORE impressive
jokes.setup: Dick calls Tommy's prank 'scum' behavior; the Dean shares his own prank fondly
jokes.punchline: The Dean — an authority figure — is not only NOT disgusted by the prank but competitive about it, implying Dick's prank was better than his marching band one
jokes.explanation: The Dean's conspiratorial enjoyment subverts the authority-figure role. Works as institutional irony.

jokes.text: I remember my own freshman prank. I messed with the marching band's formation and made 'em spell out a dirty word. / That's very funny. / Well, it's nothing like this. / Well, you're too kind.
jokes.setup: The chancellor shares his own pranking history; Dick deflects with false modesty
jokes.punchline: Dick takes 'it's nothing like this' (meant as a compliment to the chancellor's prank) and responds 'Well, you're too kind' — as if the comparison favors Dick's prank. Then the conversation pivots to social networking, breaking the expected confrontation
jokes.explanation: The rapid social escalation — Dick and the chancellor bonding over pranks, then immediately pivoting to the chancellor trying to set Dick up with his daughter — is a nice comedic acceleration. The misread of 'you're too kind' is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Such attention to detail. I love the coffee mug. / Thank you. / The coffee mug was my idea. / This whole thing is mine. He had nothing to do with it. I'm the mastermind behind the freshman prank.
jokes.setup: The chancellor admires the prank; Tommy politely thanks him
jokes.punchline: Dick immediately elbows in to claim full credit, then Tommy fights back — both trying to claim ownership of a prank that got Tommy in trouble, purely to impress the chancellor (and his daughter)
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of both Tommy and Dick competitively claiming credit for a prank that was designed to get Tommy expelled is excellent. Dick's immediate pivot from 'it was for your own good' to 'I want the credit for impressing this man' is perfectly in character. 'This whole thing is mine. He had nothing to do with it. I'm the mastermind' is an enjoyable escalation.

jokes.text: Yes! If there's anyone you should be foisting your daughter off on, it's me!
jokes.setup: The chancellor has been talking about his daughter; Tommy and Dick are competing for credit
jokes.punchline: 'Foisting your daughter off on' is Dick's accidentally accurate characterization of the chancellor's dating-app enthusiasm — and he says it with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Foisting your daughter off on' is a genuinely funny word choice — Dick's alien vocabulary misses the social grace of the situation and accidentally tells the truth about what the chancellor is doing. Character-specific and economical. Solid joke.

jokes.text: Bryce, do you wish to remain anonymous? [beat] Sally, Bryce feels that you've been sexually harassing him
jokes.setup: Harry asks if Bryce wants to remain anonymous in his harassment complaint — with Bryce sitting right there
jokes.punchline: The absurd formality of asking for anonymity while the alleged harasser is in the room, followed by immediately naming him anyway
jokes.explanation: Nice bureaucratic absurdism — the HR procedure of anonymity being applied in a situation where it's completely impossible. The gap between the question and the obvious answer (Bryce is right there) is the comedy. The pause before the reveal adds to the awkwardness.

jokes.text: I think that's something I'd like to discuss with Bryce privately. / Ok, I'll leave you 2 alone. / Harry? Would you please stay?
jokes.setup: Sally wants to speak to Bryce alone — ostensibly to address the harassment claim
jokes.punchline: Bryce immediately calls Harry back — the very act of asking for a private meeting with her harasser is itself harassment, and Bryce knows it
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured three-beat joke. Sally's request to meet alone triggers the exact dynamic she's accused of. Bryce's immediate 'Harry? Would you please stay?' is the perfect self-protective punchline. The reversal of who has power in the room — Bryce coolly managing Sally — is funny and slightly surprising. Strong economy and structure.

jokes.text: I mean, a Pat on your muscular back is not harassment.
jokes.setup: Sally attempts to gaslight Bryce about her behavior, minimizing it as 'professional encouragement'
jokes.punchline: Her defense accidentally incriminates her: she can't help noting his back is 'muscular' while arguing she doesn't see him as a sex object
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining defense is a classic comedy structure, but 'muscular back' is the specific word that makes it exceptional. Sally can't even form the sentence denying harassment without proving she's objectifying Bryce. The adjective 'muscular' inserted into an otherwise-plausible professional statement is perfect comic construction. Highly quotable. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Well, if you're not comfortable, you should take off your pants. Casual thursday.
jokes.setup: Bryce has cited state harassment law and said he's 'very uncomfortable'
jokes.punchline: Sally's response to Bryce being uncomfortable is to suggest he remove his pants — invoking the completely invented 'Casual Thursday' as institutional cover
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Casual Thursday' is an inspired invention — Sally creates a fake institutional policy on the spot to legitimize her harassment. The two-word capper delivers an enormous amount of character comedy: Sally's confidence, her complete lack of self-awareness, her resourcefulness in the service of the worst possible goals. 'Casual Thursday' as a standalone phrase is highly quotable. One of the episode's top three moments.

jokes.text: I treated you like a sexy, hunky object instead of a sexy, hunky employee, and I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Sally is apologizing for her harassment of Bryce
jokes.punchline: Her apology concedes the object/employee distinction but not the 'sexy, hunky' part — she literally cannot help describing him that way even in her sincere apology
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The parallel structure — 'sexy, hunky object' vs 'sexy, hunky employee' — is formally perfect. Sally acknowledges the ONLY problem was the noun ('object') while completely missing that the adjectives ('sexy, hunky') are themselves the issue. The apology makes the harassment worse while sounding like a genuine attempt at accountability. It's a line that rewards close attention: you realize she's apologized for nothing. Highly quotable, perfectly character-specific (only Sally Solomon would apologize this way), and the structure is elegant. This is the kind of joke a comedy writer's room would be proud of for years.

jokes.text: "I treated you like a sexy, hunky object instead of a sexy, hunky employee, and I'm sorry."
jokes.setup: Sally delivers what should be a sincere apology for sexual harassment
jokes.punchline: She corrects herself from 'object' to 'employee' while maintaining both adjectives — 'sexy, hunky' — completely undermining the apology
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. The structure is perfect: the parallel construction 'sexy, hunky object / sexy, hunky employee' with the same adjectives is brilliantly written. Sally believes she's correcting herself — she understands the conceptual distinction but doesn't realize that maintaining 'sexy, hunky' in her apology makes it not an apology at all. The joke works as: (1) a precise satire of performative apologies that don't actually acknowledge the offense, (2) perfect character comedy — Sally literally cannot see Bryce as non-sexual, (3) deeply quotable. The economy is exceptional — one parallel sentence does everything.

jokes.text: This is good. The system works. Bye-Bye, Sally.
jokes.setup: Sally has been found guilty of harassment and offered to resign; Harry responds
jokes.punchline: 'The system works' — Harry's cheerful endorsement of an HR process that just drove their colleague away, delivered with complete satisfaction
jokes.explanation: 'The system works' is a nice deadpan line — delivered without a trace of irony by Harry about a system that has just dismantled their workplace. Economy is excellent. The cheerful 'Bye-Bye, Sally' adds to the absurdity of his contentment.

jokes.text: well, no hard feelings. / Of course not. / Cool. In you go, you piece of meat!
jokes.setup: Sally says a gracious goodbye to Bryce, seemingly having learned her lesson
jokes.punchline: 'In you go, you piece of meat!' — Sally pushes Bryce into a room/car/space with full return to objectifying language, showing she learned absolutely nothing
jokes.explanation: Exceptional scene-ender. The structure is perfect: gracious farewell establishes apparent redemption arc → 'In you go, you piece of meat!' detonates it completely in five words. 'You piece of meat' is a spectacular insult that reveals Sally's objectification is entirely unresolved. The physical action ('in you go') implies she's literally shoving him somewhere. Highly quotable, perfect character integration, and the callback to her apology makes it even funnier in retrospect. One of the episode's top three jokes.

jokes.text: We're never hiring anyone ever again. / Well, with him gone, I guess you'll be wantin' me to oil up and put on the speedos. / Oh, no, no.
jokes.setup: Dick declares they'll never hire anyone again after the Bryce disaster
jokes.punchline: Harry interprets this as meaning he should now fill the 'attractive eye candy' role, offering to oil up and wear speedos — an image that horrifies Dick
jokes.explanation: Harry's logical (to an alien) deduction that he should replace Bryce's role is a great callback. 'Oil up and put on the speedos' is a funny specific image. Dick's horrified 'Oh, no, no' confirms the joke. The callback to the rooftop sunbathing scene gives this extra resonance.

jokes.text: You teach at a college. / Oh, sure. Throw that in my face.
jokes.setup: Mary/the professor character is railing against college as a 'big ugly machine' that will chew Tommy up
jokes.punchline: Tommy points out she teaches at a college; her response — 'Oh, sure. Throw that in my face' — treats a factual observation as a personal attack
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy joke. 'Oh, sure. Throw that in my face' as a response to simply being reminded of your own job is a wonderful piece of self-contradiction comedy. The character who rails against the institution they're part of, then responds to the observation with wounded pride, is a recognizable archetype executed with precision. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Yes, with your new life of learning, your internet, your nintendo, your fancy friends. Your tv, your virtual reality, your... your... and your... I... I don't even know!
jokes.setup: Mary is accusing Tommy of having changed since going to college
jokes.punchline: Her list of corrupting influences — internet, Nintendo, virtual reality — deteriorates into 'and your... I don't even know!' as she runs out of things to accuse him of
jokes.explanation: The escalation that collapses into '...I don't even know!' is a well-executed comedic structure. The list of college corruptions (Nintendo, virtual reality) is period-specific but the trailing off into helplessness is the universal joke. Good energy in the delivery as written.

jokes.text: I don't want you to go! I don't want you to go.
jokes.setup: Dick has been arguing with Tommy about college through increasingly elaborate pretexts
jokes.punchline: He finally admits the simple truth: 'I don't want you to go' — all the scheming and posturing collapses into a genuine, simple emotional confession
jokes.explanation: The emotional honesty after all the scheming is funny because of the contrast — after 'Bingo!' and all the manipulation, the real motivation is achingly simple. The repetition of the line emphasizes it. More sweet than funny, but the comedy is in how long it took to get here.

jokes.text: Why did you have to grow up? / I don't know. It was just the body I picked.
jokes.setup: Dick asks an emotional question about Tommy growing up
jokes.punchline: Tommy's alien matter-of-factness: 'I don't know. It was just the body I picked.' — treating the existential lament about growing up as a literal question about body selection
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke that works on multiple levels. Dick's emotional question is genuinely touching; Tommy's alien response ('it was just the body I picked') reframes the entire pathos of aging and growing up as a random selection process. It's both funny and unexpectedly resonant — the alien perspective accidentally illuminates something true about how arbitrary physical development feels. High character integration, great economy. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Parenting's hard. You give love, you give encouragement, you give support... and then, if you do a good job, they just go away.
jokes.setup: The emotional scene between Dick and Tommy reaches its peak
jokes.punchline: Dick's alien synthesis of parenting: the successful outcome IS loss — 'if you do a good job, they just go away' — framing parental love as inherently self-defeating
jokes.explanation: A genuinely well-written observation about parenting that works as both comedy and emotional truth. The alien perspective (stating the contradiction of parental love analytically rather than sentimentally) gives this line its edge. 'They just go away' as the result of doing a good job is funny precisely because it's true. Quotable and emotionally resonant — rare combination.

jokes.text: What do you mean? / Parental love at its best. It's the only love there is that inevitably leads to separation. / How do you always know these things? / I'm the information officer. I sent you a memo on this years ago.
jokes.setup: Dick asks how Tommy always has such wisdom
jokes.punchline: 'I'm the information officer. I sent you a memo on this years ago.' — Tommy's role-based justification for his emotional insight, and the slight dig that Dick should have known this already
jokes.explanation: Perfect character callback. Tommy's job title — which has been a running joke throughout about the absurdity of alien data gathering — is here used to explain emotional wisdom. 'I sent you a memo on this years ago' implies Dick's grief is a predictable human process that Tommy formally documented. Deflates the sentiment beautifully while also being genuinely touching. Highly quotable and smart structural work.

jokes.text: There's beer in this room.
jokes.setup: Dick and Tommy are having a quiet moment in Tommy's dorm room; Dick notices something
jokes.punchline: 'There's beer in this room.' — Dick's alien delight at discovering beer (which they gave Tommy to take to college) now available to drink, delivered as a simple factual observation
jokes.explanation: Wonderful economy — five words, delivers a full callback and character beat. Dick's alien observational pleasure at beer being present, stated as a basic fact rather than enthusiasm, is perfect deadpan. The callback to the opening beer gift is elegant. 'There's beer in this room' is one of those lines that's funnier the flatter it's delivered.

jokes.text: Nice to meet you, Joel. / Isn't this yours? / No, no, no. I was just leaving.
jokes.setup: Dick finally meets Tommy's passed-out roommate Joel, who apparently has an object that's Dick's
jokes.punchline: Dick denies ownership and immediately bails — implying he left something embarrassing in Joel's possession, or simply is caught doing something he doesn't want to explain
jokes.explanation: Quick callback to Joel the perpetually-unconscious roommate. The joke is in Dick's hasty denial and departure — something incriminating is being implied without being specified. Light but functional.

jokes.text: You came on to him, huh? / Yeah, like Germany came on to Poland.
jokes.setup: Dick asks Sally what happened with Bryce
jokes.punchline: Sally compares her sexual harassment of Bryce to Germany's invasion of Poland — a spectacularly dark and specific historical analogy for workplace harassment
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most daring and brilliantly executed joke. 'Like Germany came on to Poland' is extraordinary for several reasons: (1) It's shockingly original — no one would make this comparison. (2) It's structurally perfect: the political/military aggression maps precisely onto sexual harassment (unwanted advances, overwhelming force, zero consent). (3) It's character-specific: only Sally would casually invoke WWII to describe her own behavior and only an alien would make this comparison without shame. (4) Economy is perfect — five words (Germany came on to Poland) deliver everything. (5) It's completely earned by the episode's harassment subplot. Comparable to the 8.0 calibration anchor or above — genuinely exceptional and close to a cultural-touchstone level line. Highest scoring joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Dick misses Tommy — 'I wonder what Tommy's doing right now?' — then the cut to Tommy doing laundry
jokes.setup: Dick wonders aloud what Tommy is doing at college — implying rich college experiences
jokes.punchline: Tommy walks in — 'school's only an hour away, so I figured I could do my laundry here' — deflating the separation narrative entirely
jokes.explanation: Good structural callback to the episode's central emotional arc. The entire episode was about separation; Tommy arrives home for laundry. The anti-climax is well-earned and well-structured — the setup has been built over 20 minutes.

jokes.text: I wonder what Tommy's doing right now? / He's separating his whites. / Yeah, and maybe starting to presoak. / Mmm. I hope he goes easy on the bleach, but you know Tommy. He won't. / No. Never.
jokes.setup: The team muses about Tommy at college; Tommy is literally just in the next room doing laundry
jokes.punchline: The team's speculation about Tommy's great college adventures turns out to be accurate literal laundry descriptions — they're imagining his laundry process as grand independent endeavors, and they're right in the worst possible way
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke and a structural masterpiece. The team fantasizes reverently about Tommy's new independent life, but because we just learned he's doing laundry in the next room, every line of speculation is simultaneously heartfelt and deflating. 'I hope he goes easy on the bleach, but you know Tommy. He won't. No. Never.' — spoken with complete solemnity about a man's bleach habits — is both absurd and genuinely sweet. The callback to the laundry reveal makes the whole sequence land with compound impact. Perfect ending construction. Among the episode's very best moments.

tmdb_overview: Criss and Liz decide to celebrate Valentine's Day, but they need to buy a dining room table first. Jack entertains his mother-in-law, Diana, as Jenna frantically looks to Pete to fill in last-minute as the producer of her first live performance on "America's Kidz Got Singing." Back at the office, Tracy and Frank try to help Lutz find someone to spend Valentine's with.
insight: Season 6 dips to 73.9 as escalation-heavy episode trades sharpness for absurdist sprawl.
